Prayer, praise, and wisdom for life.

Twelve short books, from Assyria to the return from exile.

1.resume: Genesis tells the story of how everything began: the world, humanity, sin, and God's plan to save. After eleven chapters on origins, the narrative narrows to one family—Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph—through whom God promises to bless all nations.
1.auteur: The book does not name its author. Jewish and Christian tradition attributes it to Moses, as well as the four books that follow; Jesus calls this collection
1.date: Written in the time of Moses, around 1446–1406 BC. The narrative spans an enormous period: from creation until Joseph's death in Egypt, around 1805 BC.
1.destinataires: The people of Israel who came out of Egypt, who needed to know where they came from, who their God was, and why they were headed toward Canaan.
1.contexte:
The word "Genesis" comes from Greek and means "origin." The book lays the foundation for all of Scripture: God the Creator, mankind made in His image (Genesis 1:27), the Fall and its consequences (Genesis 3:6), the Flood, Babel.

Beginning in chapter 12, God calls Abram and makes him a three-part promise: a land, a numerous offspring, and a blessing for all the families of the earth (Genesis 12:3). The rest of the Bible tells how this promise is fulfilled. The book ends in Egypt, where Jacob's family took refuge during a famine: the stage for Exodus is set.
plan: Joseph, from Slavery to the Palace
themes: Everything that exists comes from God's word, and what he made was “very good” (Genesis 1:31).
Disobedience breaks the relationship with God, but God never stops seeking man: “Where are you?” (Genesis 3:9).
With Noah and then with Abraham, God binds himself by promises he will keep no matter what.
Even the evil that people do, God can turn into good (Genesis 50:20).

versets.t: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.
So God created man in His own image; in the image of God He created him; male and female He created them.

I will make you a great nation; I will bless you and make your name great; and you shall be a blessing. I will bless those who bless you, and I will curse him who curses you; and in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed.
And Abram believed the Lord, and He accounted it to him for righteousness.
But as for you, you meant evil against me; but God meant it for good, in order to bring it about as it is this day, to save many people alive.

1.christ: From the Fall onward, God announces that a descendant of the woman will crush the serpent's head (Genesis 3:15): this is the first promise of a Savior. The ram provided in Isaac's place (Genesis 22:13) foreshadows the Lamb given in our place, and Paul shows that the "offspring" promised to Abraham is Christ (Galatians 3:16).

2.resume: Israel is enslaved in Egypt. God calls Moses, strikes Egypt with ten plagues, leads His people out through the Red Sea, makes a covenant with them at Sinai, and comes to dwell among them in the tabernacle.
2.auteur: Moses, according to Jewish and Christian tradition. The book itself mentions that Moses wrote down the words of the Lord (Exodus 24:4).
2.date: Written in the time of Moses. The narrative spans approximately eighty years, from his birth (around 1526 BC) to the erection of the tabernacle, one year after the exodus from Egypt (around 1445 BC).
2.destinataires: The people of Israel in the wilderness, so they might remember their deliverance and live according to the covenant.
2.contexte:
About four centuries after Joseph, the descendants of Jacob have become a numerous people. A new king "who did not know Joseph" (Exodus 1:8) reduces them to slavery. God hears their cries, remembers His covenant with Abraham (Exodus 2:24), and calls Moses from a burning bush.

The book unfolds in three movements: deliverance (the plagues, Passover, the Red Sea), the covenant at Sinai (the Ten Commandments), and God's presence among His people in the tabernacle. It ends with the glory of the Lord filling the tent (Exodus 40:34).
plan: Slavery and the Call of Moses
The Red Sea and the Wilderness
themes: God sees the suffering of His people and intervenes with power to set them free (Exodus 3:7).
"I AM WHO I AM": God reveals Himself as the one who exists by Himself and remains faithful (Exodus 3:14).
The Ten Commandments are not a pathway to salvation: they are given to a people already delivered (Exodus 20:2).
The tabernacle allows a holy God to dwell in the midst of His people (Exodus 25:8).

versets.t: God said to Moses, "I AM WHO I AM." And He said, "Thus you shall say to the children of Israel, 'I AM has sent me to you.'"

versets.ref: The blood shall be a sign for you on the houses where you are. And when I see the blood, I will pass over you; and the plague shall not be on you to destroy you when I strike the land of Egypt.
versets.t: The Lord will fight for you, and you shall hold your peace.

versets.ref: The Lord is my strength and my song; He also has become my salvation. He is my God, and I will praise Him; My father's God, and I will exalt Him.
versets.t: Exodus 20:2-3

versets.ref: I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage. You shall have no other gods before Me.

2.christ: Jesus is the Lamb of the Passover: "Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed" (1 Corinthians 5:7). He takes up the divine name "I AM" (John 8:58), and John writes that the Word "dwelt" among us (John 1:14): the Greek word evokes a tent pitched, like the tabernacle in the midst of Israel.

3.resume: How can a sinful people live with a holy God in their midst? Leviticus answers: through sacrifices, through the ministry of the priests, and through a holy life in every area.
3.auteur: Moses, according to tradition. More than thirty times, the book states that
3.date: Given at the foot of Mount Sinai, in the month following the erection of the tabernacle, around 1445 BC.
3.destinataires: The people of Israel, and especially the priests of the tribe of Levi—from which the book takes its name.
3.contexte:
The tabernacle has just been set up at the end of Exodus. Leviticus explains how to approach it: five kinds of sacrifices, the consecration of Aaron and his sons, rules of clean and unclean, and holiness that touches food, family, work, and justice.

The heart of the book is the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:30), when the high priest entered the Most Holy Place once a year. Leviticus is not just a list of rituals: it also contains
themes: « Soyez saints, car je suis saint » : la vie entière appartient à Dieu (Lévitique 19:2).
Life is in the blood, and it is the blood that makes atonement (Leviticus 17:11).
God himself opens a way for the sinner to draw near to him.
Israel's calendar marks the year by remembering God's works (Leviticus 23:2).

versets.t: For on this day atonement shall be made for you, to cleanse you; you shall be clean from all your sins before the Lord.
For the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it to you upon the altar to make atonement for your souls; for it is the blood that makes atonement for the soul.
Speak to all the congregation of the children of Israel, and say to them: You shall be holy, for I the Lord your God am holy.
You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people, but you shall love your neighbor as yourself: I am the Lord.

4.resume: The people leave Sinai for the promised land, but at Kadesh they refuse to enter. An entire generation dies in the wilderness for forty years, and God prepares the next one to inherit the promise.
4.auteur: Moses, according to tradition; the book specifies that he wrote down the stages of the journey (Numbers 33:2).
4.date: The narrative spans nearly thirty-nine years, from the departure from Sinai (around 1445 BC) to the plains of Moab, facing Jericho (around 1406 BC).
4.destinataires: The new generation of Israel, about to enter Canaan, so they would not repeat the unbelief of their fathers.
4.contexte:
The book's name comes from two censuses of the people (chapters 1 and 26). Between them, an entire generation has perished. At Kadesh, the twelve spies return from the promised land: ten discourage the people, but only Joshua and Caleb call for faith in God (Numbers 14:8-9). The people refuse to enter, and God condemns them to wander for forty years.

It is a book of complaints and rebellions—Korah, and even Moses at Meribah (Numbers 20:12)—but above all of God's faithfulness, who feeds His people, protects them, and turns the curse that Balaam was to pronounce into a blessing (Numbers 23:20).
plan: The census and the organization of the camp
From Sinai to Kadesh: the complaints
themes: To refuse to believe God is to miss what he has prepared (Numbers 14:11).
God is not a man that he should lie: what he has said, he accomplishes (Numbers 23:19).
God puts his name on his people to bless them and keep them (Numbers 6:27).

versets.t: The Lord bless you and keep you; the Lord make His face shine upon you and be gracious to you; the Lord lift up His countenance upon you and give you peace.
Only do not rebel against the Lord, and do not fear the people of the land, for they are our bread; their protection has departed from them, and the Lord is with us. Do not fear them.
Then the Lord said to Moses, 'Make a fiery serpent, and set it on a pole; and it shall be that everyone who is bitten, when he looks at it, shall live.'
God is not a man, that He should lie, nor a son of man, that He should repent. Has He said, and will He not do? Or has He spoken, and will He not make it good?

4.christ: Jesus applies the bronze serpent to Himself: 'And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of Man be lifted up' (John 3:14). Paul also sees in Christ the spiritual rock that accompanied Israel and gave them water (1 Corinthians 10:4).

5.resume: Before he dies, Moses recites the law to the generation about to enter the land. He recalls their history, re-explains the commandments, and calls the people to love the Lord with all their heart.
5.auteur: The discourses are from Moses, who wrote this law (Deuteronomy 31:9). The account of his death in the final chapter was added after him; Jewish tradition attributes it to Joshua.
5.date: Spoken in the plains of Moab, in the final months of Moses' life, in the fortieth year after the exodus from Egypt (Deuteronomy 1:3), around 1406 B.C.
5.destinataires: The generation born in the wilderness, ready to cross the Jordan.
5.contexte:
"Deuteronomy" means "second law"—not a different law, but the law repeated to a new generation. Moses, who will not enter the land, delivers three major addresses, then blesses the tribes and climbs Mount Nebo to view the promised land.

The tone is that of a father saying goodbye. It contains Israel's great confession of faith: "Hear, O Israel! The Lord our God, the Lord is one" (Deuteronomy 6:4). It is also the book Jesus quotes three times to answer the devil in the wilderness (Matthew 4:4).
themes: Obedience flows from the heart: love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength (Deuteronomy 6:5).
Forgetting what God has done is the first step toward unfaithfulness (Deuteronomy 8:11).
Life and death are set before the people: they must choose life (Deuteronomy 30:19).
Faith is passed down in the home by speaking God's Word to your children (Deuteronomy 6:7).

versets.t: Hear, O Israel! The Lord our God, the Lord is one. You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength.
Know therefore that the Lord your God, He is God, the faithful God who keeps covenant and mercy for a thousand generations with those who love Him and keep His commandments.

He humbled you and let you hunger and fed you with manna, which you did not know and which your fathers did not know, that He might make you know that man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of the Lord.
Be strong and courageous! Do not be afraid or terrified because of them; for the Lord your God goes with you, He will not leave you or forsake you.

5.christ: Moses announces: "The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers" (Deuteronomy 18:15). Peter affirms that this prophet is Jesus (Acts 3:22). And Jesus, tempted in the wilderness, lived what Israel had failed to live: sustaining himself by every word that comes from the mouth of God.

6.resume: Under Joshua's leadership, Israel crosses the Jordan River, takes Jericho, and conquers the land of Canaan. The land is then divided among the twelve tribes, and Joshua calls the people to remain faithful.
6.auteur: The book does not name its author. Jewish tradition attributes it to Joshua himself, who "wrote these things in the Book of the Law of God" (Joshua 24:26); the account of his death was added later.
6.date: The events take place around 1406–1380 BC, from the entry into Canaan to Joshua's death.
6.destinataires: The people of Israel settled in the land, so they may know that their land is a gift from God.
6.contexte:
Moses has died; Joshua, his servant, takes over. God promises him: "I will be with you" (Joshua 1:5). The people cross the Jordan on dry ground, watch the walls of Jericho fall, then conquer the land in three campaigns: in the center, in the south, and in the north.

The second half of the book describes the division of the land among the tribes, including the cities of refuge and the cities of the Levites. The book concludes with a solemn call to choose whom to serve: "As for me and my household, we will serve the Lord" (Joshua 24:15).
themes: Not one of all the good promises the Lord had made failed; all were fulfilled (Joshua 21:45).
Joshua's courage comes from the Word meditated on day and night (Joshua 1:8).
Achan's hidden sin causes the whole people to stumble at Ai (Joshua 7:1).
Each generation must choose in turn to serve the Lord (Joshua 24:15).

versets.t: Keep this Book of the Law always on your lips; meditate on it day and night, so that you may be careful to do everything written in it. Then you will be prosperous and successful.
Have I not commanded you? Be strong and courageous. Do not be afraid; do not be discouraged, for the Lord your God will be with you wherever you go.
Not one of all the good promises the Lord had made to Israel failed; every one was fulfilled.

But if serving the Lord seems undesirable to you, then choose for yourselves this day whom you will serve, whether the gods your ancestors served beyond the River, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land you are living. But as for me and my household, we will serve the Lord.

6.christ: Joshua and Jesus share the same name in Hebrew, which means: the Lord saves. Where Joshua gave the people a temporary rest, Jesus offers true rest (Hebrews 4:8–9). And Rahab, the foreigner saved by her faith, enters the genealogy of Christ (Matthew 1:5).

7.accroche: Everyone Did What Was Right in Their Own Eyes
7.resume: After Joshua, Israel turns away from God, falls under oppression, cries out for help, and God raises up liberators — the judges. The cycle repeats, growing darker and darker, until a people without direction.
7.auteur: The book does not name its author; Jewish tradition attributes it to Samuel. The remark "In those days there was no king in Israel" suggests it was written in the early days of the monarchy.
7.date: The narrative spans approximately three centuries, from Joshua's death until the time of Samuel (around 1380–1050 BC).
7.destinataires: Israel at the beginning of the monarchy, to show them the devastation of unfaithfulness and their need for a king according to God.
7.contexte:
After Joshua, a generation arises "who did not know the Lord" (Judges 2:10). The book describes a cycle that repeats itself: Israel abandons God, God delivers them to their enemies, the people cry out, God raises up a deliverer — a "judge" — and the land enjoys peace… until it falls back.

Twelve judges succeed one another, from Othniel to Samson, passing through Deborah, Gideon, and Jephthah. The book goes from bad to worse and ends with terrible accounts that reveal a people without direction. The key phrase returns like a refrain: "everyone did what was right in their own eyes" (Judges 21:25).
themes: Forgetting God leads to slavery; each generation must know Him for itself (Judges 2:10).
At every cry of the people, God responds by raising up a deliverer (Judges 2:18).
Gideon, the smallest of his family, saves Israel with three hundred men (Judges 7:7).
The final disorder makes people hope for a righteous king to lead the people.

versets.t: Then the Lord raised up judges, who saved them out of the hand of those who plundered them.
And the Angel of the Lord appeared to him and said to him, "The Lord is with you, mighty man of valor!"
And the Lord said to Gideon, "By the three hundred men who lapped I will save you, and deliver the Midianites into your hand. Let all the other people go, every man to his home."
In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes.

7.christ: Each judge is an imperfect and temporary savior, and several fall themselves. The book creates longing for a liberator who will never fall: Jesus, the righteous One who saves once and for all. Yet Hebrews lists Gideon, Barak, Samson, and Jephthah among the witnesses of faith (Hebrews 11:32).

8.accroche: Faithfulness in the Time of the Judges
8.resume: A Moabite widow, Ruth, clings to her mother-in-law Naomi and to her God. In Bethlehem, she finds a redeemer, Boaz, and becomes the great-grandmother of King David.
8.auteur: The book does not name its author; Jewish tradition attributes it to Samuel. It ends with the genealogy of David, which places its writing no earlier than David's reign.
8.date: The story takes place "in the days of the judges" (Ruth 1:1), around 1100 BC.
8.destinataires: Israel, to whom the book shows that God's faithfulness reaches also through the small and the foreigners.
8.contexte:
During a famine, Elimelech leaves Bethlehem for the land of Moab with his wife Naomi and their two sons. The three men die there. Ruth, the Moabite daughter-in-law, refuses to abandon Naomi: "Your people will be my people, and your God my God" (Ruth 1:16).

In Bethlehem, Ruth gleans in the field of Boaz, a relative of Elimelech. Boaz agrees to play the role of "redeemer": he redeems the family's field and marries Ruth. Their son Obed will be the grandfather of David (Ruth 4:17). In the midst of the darkness of the Judges, this little book is a light.
plan: The Departure and Return to Bethlehem
Ruth in the Field of Boaz
The Night on the Threshing Floor
The Redemption and the Birth of Obed
themes: Ruth commits herself to Naomi and to her God, expecting nothing in return (Ruth 1:16).
What seems like chance—the field where Ruth goes to glean—is directed by God (Ruth 2:3).
The kinsman-redeemer redeems what was lost and restores the family name (Ruth 4:10).
A foreigner finds refuge under the wings of the God of Israel (Ruth 2:12).

versets.t: Ruth replied: Do not urge me to leave you, to turn back from following you. Where you go I will go, and where you live I will live; your people will be my people, and your God my God.
May the Lord repay you for what you have done. May you be richly rewarded by the Lord, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to take refuge!
The women said to Naomi: "Praise be to the Lord, who has not left you without a family redeemer. May he become famous throughout Israel!

8.christ: Boaz, the relative who redeems, is a beautiful picture of Christ, our Redeemer. And Ruth, the foreigner, enters into the line of the Messiah (Matthew 1:5): already, God's grace transcends the boundaries of Israel.

9.resume: Samuel, the child given in answer to Hannah's prayer, becomes the last of the judges. The people demand a king: Saul is chosen then rejected, and God secretly anoints a young shepherd, David.
9.auteur: The book does not name its author. Samuel could only have written the beginning, since he dies in chapter 25. The writings of Samuel, Nathan, and Gad are cited as sources for this history (1 Chronicles 29:29). 1 and 2 Samuel were originally one single book.
9.date: The narrative spans roughly a century, from Samuel's birth to Saul's death (around 1100–1010 BC).
9.destinataires: Israel under the monarchy, to understand how God established the house of David.
9.contexte:
Israel experiences the end of the time of the Judges. Hannah, a barren woman, prays and receives a son, Samuel, who becomes a prophet, priest, and judge. But the people demand a king "like all the nations have" (1 Samuel 8:5). God gives them Saul, tall and impressive, but he disobeys.

God then chooses the youngest of Jesse's sons, for "man looks at the outward appearance, but the Lord looks at the heart" (1 Samuel 16:7). The story continues with David's victory over Goliath, his friendship with Jonathan, and the years he flees from Saul without ever raising his hand against him. The book ends with Saul and his sons' death on Mount Gilboa.
plan: Hannah and the Birth of Samuel
themes: God does not choose according to appearance, but according to the heart (1 Samuel 16:7).
Obeying is better than sacrifices (1 Samuel 15:22).
Hannah's song praises the God who overthrows the proud and lifts up the poor (1 Samuel 2:8).
David refuses to lay a hand on Saul, even when Saul is at his mercy (1 Samuel 24:7).

versets.t: Then the Lord came and stood and called as at other times, "Samuel, Samuel!" And Samuel answered, "Speak, for Your servant is listening."

So Samuel said: "Does the Lord have as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the Lord? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to heed than the fat of rams."

But the Lord said to Samuel, "Do not look at his appearance or at his physical stature, because I have rejected him. For the Lord does not see as man sees; for man looks at the outward appearance, but the Lord looks at the heart."

Then David said to the Philistine, "You come to me with a sword, with a spear, and with a javelin. But I come to you in the name of the Lord of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have taunted."

9.christ: David, the shepherd of Bethlehem anointed by God then rejected before he reigns, prefigures Jesus, "Son of David," himself born in Bethlehem. Hannah's song already speaks of the Lord who will give strength "to His king" and exalt the horn "of His anointed" (1 Samuel 2:10)—in Hebrew, His Messiah.

10.resume: David becomes king, makes Jerusalem his capital, and receives from God the promise of an eternal throne. Then he falls with Bathsheba, and the book unflinchingly tells his repentance and the tragedies that strike his family.
10.auteur: The book does not name its author. It draws on the writings of the prophets Nathan and Gad, who were David's contemporaries (1 Chronicles 29:29).
10.date: The narrative covers the forty years of David's reign, around 1010–970 B.C.
10.destinataires: Israel, to show them both the greatness of the promise made to David and the reality of sin, even in a king after God's own heart.
10.contexte:
After Saul's death, David first reigns seven and a half years in Hebron over Judah, then thirty-three years in Jerusalem over all Israel (2 Samuel 5:5). He brings the ark there, and God makes him an immense promise: his house and kingdom will be established forever (2 Samuel 7:16).

But the book hides nothing: the adultery with Bathsheba, the murder of Uriah, then the violence that settles in his family—Amnon, Absalom, the rebellion against his father. Confronted by the prophet Nathan, David does not excuse himself:
plan: Jerusalem, the ark, and the covenant
His final songs and the census
themes: God promises that a descendant of David will reign forever (2 Samuel 7:16).
Even the greatest king falls; what matters is returning to God (2 Samuel 12:13).
Forgiveness is real, but the evil sown leaves wounds (2 Samuel 12:10).
David welcomes Mephibosheth, Jonathan's disabled son, to his table (2 Samuel 9:7).

versets.t: Your house and your kingdom will be established forever before you; your throne will be established forever.
David said to Nathan, "I have sinned against the Lord!" And Nathan said to David, "The Lord has taken away your sin; you shall not die.

He said: "The Lord is my rock and my fortress and my deliverer; My God, my strength, in whom I will trust; My shield and the horn of my salvation, my stronghold. I call upon the Lord, who is worthy to be praised; So shall I be saved from my enemies.

10.christ: The promise made to David (2 Samuel 7:12-16) is the foundation of hope in the Messiah: a descendant of David will reign forever. The angel Gabriel echoes it concerning Jesus: "the Lord God will give him the throne of his father David" (Luke 1:32).

11.resume: Solomon, the wise king, builds the temple in Jerusalem. But his heart turns away, and after him the kingdom splits in two. In the north, under Ahab and Jezebel, God raises up the prophet Elijah.
11.auteur: The book does not name its author; Jewish tradition attributes it to Jeremiah. It cites its sources, such as "the book of the acts of Solomon" (1 Kings 11:41) and the chronicles of the kings of Israel and Judah. 1 and 2 Kings were originally one book, completed during the exile.
11.date: The narrative covers approximately one hundred twenty years, from Solomon's rise to power (around 970 BC) to the reign of Ahaziah, son of Ahab (around 850 BC).
11.destinataires: The Jewish people in exile in Babylon, who sought to understand how they had come to this.
11.contexte:
Solomon succeeds David, asks God for a discerning heart, and builds the temple in Jerusalem: this is Israel's golden age. But his many wives turn his heart away to other gods (1 Kings 11:4).

At his death, around 931 BC, the kingdom divides in two: in the north, Israel and its ten tribes, under Jeroboam; in the south, Judah and Jerusalem, under Rehoboam. Each king is judged by a single standard: did he do what is right in the sight of the Lord? In the midst of the north's decline, God raises up Elijah, the prophet of fire on Mount Carmel (1 Kings 18:39).
plan: The Glory and Fall of Solomon
themes: Solomon asks for a heart that knows how to listen and discern between good and evil (1 Kings 3:9).
God cannot be contained by any house, and yet He listens to the prayer of His people there (1 Kings 8:27).
You cannot limp on both sides: you must choose between the Lord and Baal (1 Kings 18:21).
God speaks to Elijah not in fire or storm, but in a soft and gentle whisper (1 Kings 19:12).

versets.t: Therefore give to your servant an understanding heart to judge your people, that I may discern between good and evil. For who is able to judge this great people of yours?
But will God indeed dwell on the earth? Behold, heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain you; how much less this house that I have built!
Then Elijah came near to all the people and said, "How long will you waver between two opinions? If the Lord is God, follow him; but if Baal, then follow him." The people did not answer him a word.
And after the earthquake came a fire; but the Lord was not in the fire. And after the fire came a gentle whisper.

11.christ: Jesus presents himself as "greater than Solomon" (Matthew 12:42) and designates his own body as the true temple (John 2:21). Elijah, meanwhile, was expected as the one who would prepare the Lord's coming, and it is John the Baptist who came "in the spirit and power of Elijah" (Luke 1:17).

12.resume: Elisha succeeds Elijah. Despite the warnings of the prophets, Israel and then Judah sink deeper into idolatry: Samaria falls to Assyria, then Jerusalem falls to Babylon.
12.auteur: The same anonymous author as 1 Kings (Jewish tradition attributes it to Jeremiah). The book was completed during the exile in Babylon.
12.date: The narrative spans nearly three centuries, from Elijah and Elisha (around 850 B.C.) to the liberation of King Jehoiachin in Babylon (around 561 B.C.).
12.destinataires: The Jews deported to Babylon, to show them that exile was not an accident but the fruit of long unfaithfulness—and that God had not forgotten the house of David.
12.contexte:
Elijah is taken up to heaven in a whirlwind, and Elisha takes up his mantle. The book follows the two kingdoms in parallel. Israel, the northern kingdom, sinks deeper into idolatry: in 722 B.C., the king of Assyria captures Samaria and deports the ten tribes (2 Kings 17:6).

Judah lasts longer, thanks to faithful kings like Hezekiah and Josiah, under whom the Book of the Law is found in the temple. But the people do not truly return. In 586 B.C., Nebuchadnezzar destroys Jerusalem and the temple. Yet the book ends on a note of hope: King Jehoiachin, a captive, is released from prison in Babylon (2 Kings 25:27).
plan: Jehu and the Kings of North and South
themes: God warns relentlessly through his prophets before judging (2 Kings 17:13).
Those who are with us are more than those who are with them (2 Kings 6:16).
The reading of the Book of the Law shakes Josiah and triggers a revival (2 Kings 22:11).
Even in exile, David's line survives (2 Kings 25:27).

versets.t: He answered, "Do not fear, for those who are with us are greater in number than those who are with them."

The Lord warned Israel and Judah by every prophet and every seer, saying, "Turn from your evil ways and keep my commandments and my statutes, in accordance with all the Law that I commanded your fathers and that I sent to you by my servants the prophets."

Before Josiah, there was no king like him who turned to the Lord with all his heart, with all his soul, and with all his might, according to all the Law of Moses; and after him none like him appeared.

12.christ: The miracles of Elisha—the widow provided for, the child raised from the dead, Naaman healed—foreshadow those of Jesus, who himself mentions Naaman in Nazareth (Luke 4:27). And the survival of the line of David, with Jehoiachin, keeps open the promise of the King to come: Jehoiachin (Coniah) appears in the genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:12).

13.resume: After lengthy genealogies spanning from Adam to the return from exile, the book focuses on David: his reign, his love for the ark, and the preparation of the temple that Solomon will build.
13.auteur: The book does not name its author; Jewish tradition attributes it to Ezra, the scribe. Chronicles shares his style, and 2 Chronicles ends with the edict of Cyrus that opens the book of Ezra.
13.date: Written after the return from exile, probably in the 5th century B.C. The account spans from the genealogies of the origins to David's death (around 970 B.C.).
13.destinataires: The Jews who had returned from Babylon, few in number and without a king, who wondered if God had abandoned them.
13.contexte:
Chronicles retells the history already recorded by Samuel and Kings, but for a different audience and with a different perspective. The author reminds the returnees where they come from: the first nine chapters are genealogies, from Adam to the inhabitants of Jerusalem at the time of the return from exile. The message is clear: you are still God's people.

The book then focuses on David, especially on what he did for worship: he brings the ark up to Jerusalem with rejoicing, organizes the Levites, the singers, and the gatekeepers, and gathers the materials that Solomon will use to build the temple.
plan: The genealogies, from Adam to the return
The death of Saul and the rise of David
themes: The genealogies remind us that God knows each family by name.
Praise is organized, joyful, and at the center of the people's life (1 Chronicles 16:34).
The throne promised to David's descendants will be established forever (1 Chronicles 17:14).
In the middle of a genealogy, Jabez's prayer shows that God answers (1 Chronicles 4:10).

versets.t: Jabez called on the God of Israel, saying, "Oh, that You would bless me indeed, and enlarge my territory, that Your hand would be with me, and that You would keep me from evil, so that I may not cause pain!" So God granted him what he requested.
Oh, give thanks to the Lord, for He is good! For His mercy endures forever.

Yours, O Lord, is the greatness and the power and the glory, the victory and the majesty; for all that is in heaven and in earth is Yours; Yours is the kingdom, O Lord, and You are exalted as head over all.

13.christ: The genealogies in Chronicles form the framework for those in Matthew and Luke: they demonstrate that Jesus is indeed the descendant of Abraham, Judah, and David who was promised. The promise of a throne "established forever" (1 Chronicles 17:14) awaits His King.

14.accroche: The Kings of Judah and the Temple
14.resume: From Solomon to exile, the book follows the kings of Judah, the line of David. It highlights spiritual awakenings and ends with Cyrus's decree that allows the return.
14.auteur: The same anonymous author as 1 Chronicles; Jewish tradition attributes it to Ezra.
14.date: Written after the return from exile, probably in the fifth century BC. The narrative spans from Solomon's reign (around 970 BC) to Cyrus's decree (538 BC).
14.destinataires: The Jews who returned from Babylon, invited to rebuild their lives around the temple and faithfulness to God.
14.contexte:
The book opens with Solomon and the dedication of the temple, where fire comes down from heaven and the glory of the Lord fills the house (2 Chronicles 7:1). After the kingdom divides, it follows only Judah, the kingdom of David's line, and largely sets aside the kings of the north.

The author emphasizes spiritual awakenings: Asa, Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah, and Josiah bring the people back to God, and each time God responds. Even Manasseh, the worst of the kings, humbles himself in captivity and God hears him (2 Chronicles 33:12-13). The book ends with Cyrus's decree: the story is not over.
themes: If my people humble themselves, pray and seek my face, I will hear them (2 Chronicles 7:14).
The eyes of the Lord run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to show himself strong on behalf of those whose heart is loyal to him (2 Chronicles 16:9).
Facing a vast army, Jehoshaphat hears: it is not you who will fight (2 Chronicles 20:15).
Every sincere return to God opens a season of blessing.

versets.t: if My people who are called by My name will humble themselves, and pray and seek My face, and turn from their wicked ways, then I will hear from heaven, and will forgive their sin and heal their land.

For the eyes of the Lord run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to show Himself strong on behalf of those whose heart is loyal to Him. In this you have done foolishly; therefore from now on you shall have wars.

And Jahaziel said, "Listen, all you of Judah and you inhabitants of Jerusalem, and you, King Jehoshaphat! Thus says the Lord to you: 'Do not be afraid nor be dismayed because of this great multitude, for the battle is not yours, but God's.

14.christ: In the Hebrew Bible, Chronicles is the final book. Jesus sums up the history of rejected prophets, from the first to the last book this way: "from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah" (Luke 11:51)—that Zechariah who was stoned in the temple courtyard (2 Chronicles 24:21). The book closes with a temple to be rebuilt and a king absent: Jesus comes to fill that void.

15.resume: Cyrus authorizes the Jews to return to Jerusalem. A first group rebuilds the temple despite opposition; years later, the scribe Ezra arrives to teach the law.
15.auteur: Ezra, a priest and scribe, according to Jewish tradition. From the end of chapter 7 onward, he narrates in the first person. Ezra and Nehemiah formed a single book in the Hebrew Bible.
15.date: The narrative spans approximately eighty years: the first return in 538 B.C., the completion of the temple in 516 B.C., then Ezra's arrival in 458 B.C.
15.destinataires: The Jewish community returned from exile, in Jerusalem and Judah.
15.contexte:
As Jeremiah had announced, God stirs the spirit of Cyrus, king of Persia, who authorizes the Jews to return and rebuild the temple (Ezra 1:1). A first group returns with Zerubbabel and the priest Joshua. The foundations are laid with joy and tears (Ezra 3:12), but opposition from neighbors halts the work for years. The prophets Haggai and Zechariah energize the people, and the temple is completed (Ezra 6:15).

Nearly sixty years later, Ezra arrives with a second group. He had "set his heart to study and to practice the law of the Lord" (Ezra 7:10). He discovers that many have intermarried with idolatrous peoples, and he leads the people to repentance.
plan: Cyrus's Edict and the First Return
themes: God fulfills Jeremiah's word by touching the heart of a pagan king (Ezra 1:1).
The temple is rebuilt despite poverty and opposition (Ezra 6:14).
To study, practice, and teach: Ezra's order remains a model (Ezra 7:10).
Ezra identifies himself with the sin of the people and confesses it before God (Ezra 9:6).

versets.t: They sang, celebrating and praising the Lord with these words: "For He is good, for His mercy toward Israel endures forever!" And all the people shouted with great joy, celebrating the Lord, because the foundation of the house of the Lord was being laid.
For Ezra had set his heart to study and practice the law of the Lord, and to teach the statutes and ordinances among Israel.

I would have been ashamed to ask the king for an escort and horsemen to protect us against the enemy on the road, for we had said to the king: "The hand of our God is for good on all those who seek Him, but His power and His wrath are against all those who abandon Him."

15.christ: Return from exile is a real but incomplete deliverance: the people have come home, yet they remain under foreign rule without a king. The prophets of return point toward a more glorious temple and a deeper return—one that Jesus brings by restoring humanity to God.

16.resume: Nehemiah, cupbearer to the king of Persia, obtains permission to return to Jerusalem to rebuild its walls. Despite threats, the work is completed in fifty-two days, then the reading of the Law brings about a profound renewal.
16.auteur: Nehemiah, who tells much of the book in the first person (Nehemiah 1:1).
16.date: From the twentieth year of King Artaxerxes, in 445 B.C. (Nehemiah 2:1), until Nehemiah's second visit, around 432 B.C. (Nehemiah 13:6).
16.destinataires: The Jewish community returned from exile, called to live as a people of the covenant.
16.contexte:
Nehemiah is cupbearer to the king of Persia at Susa. When he hears that the walls of Jerusalem remain in ruins, he weeps, fasts, and prays for days (Nehemiah 1:4). The king sends him as governor. Despite the mockery and threats of Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem, the walls are rebuilt in fifty-two days (Nehemiah 6:15).

Ezra then reads the Law publicly before all the people, who weep as they hear it. Nehemiah responds to them:
plan: The Reading of the Law and Renewal
themes: Nehemiah prays before speaking to the king, then he acts with method (Nehemiah 2:4-5).
Facing threats, they work with one hand and hold a weapon with the other (Nehemiah 4:17).
The reading of the law, explained to the people, brings about repentance and joy (Nehemiah 8:8).
The joy of the Lord is the strength of His people (Nehemiah 8:10).

versets.t: So I answered them, "The God of heaven Himself will give us success. We His servants will arise and build, but you have no share, nor right, nor remembrance in Jerusalem."
So they read distinctly from the Book of the Law of God, and they explained the meaning so that the people understood what was read.

Then he said to them, "Go your way, eat the fat, drink the sweet, and send portions to those for whom nothing is prepared; for this day is holy to our Lord. Do not sorrow, for the joy of the Lord is your strength."

16.christ: Nehemiah leaves the king's palace to come and raise up his people in ruins: an echo of Him who "emptied Himself" to come to us (Philippians 2:7). But his reforms lose momentum the moment he is absent: only a new heart is needed, which only Christ can give.

17.resume: A young Jewish woman becomes queen of Persia. When a decree threatens to annihilate her people, Esther risks her life before the king, and the plot turns against its author.
17.auteur: The book does not name its author. It comes from a Persian Jew who was well acquainted with court life; tradition has proposed Mordecai, who wrote down these events (Esther 9:20).
17.date: The events take place under King Ahasuerus (Xerxes I), around 483–473 BC, between the first return under Zerubbabel and the coming of Ezra.
17.destinataires: The Jews who remained in exile in the Persian Empire, and all those who celebrate the Feast of Purim.
17.contexte:
The story takes place in Susa, the capital of the Persian Empire. Esther, a young Jewish orphan raised by her cousin Mordecai, becomes queen without revealing her origins. Haman, the prime minister, obtains a decree to annihilate all the Jews in the empire.

Esther risks her life by presenting herself before the king without being summoned. Mordecai had told her: "Who knows whether you have come to the kingdom for such a time as this?" (Esther 4:14). The plot turns against Haman, and the Jews are saved: this is the origin of the Feast of Purim. Remarkable fact: the name of God does not appear even once in the book—and yet His hand is everywhere.
plan: Deliverance and the Feast of Purim
themes: A sleepless night of the king changes the course of history (Esther 6:1).
"If I perish, I perish": Esther dares to save her people (Esther 4:16).
The proud falls into the trap he had prepared (Esther 7:10).
God places his children where they can serve his purpose (Esther 4:14).

versets.t: For if you remain silent at this time, relief and deliverance will arise for the Jews from another place; but you and your father's house will perish. And who knows whether you have come to the kingdom for such a time as this?

Go, gather all the Jews who are present in Susa, and fast for me; do not eat or drink for three days, night or day. My maids and I will fast likewise. And so I will go to the king, which is against the law; and if I perish, I perish.

17.christ: Esther intercedes at the risk of her life for a condemned people. Jesus goes further: He does not merely risk His life, He gives it, and He is "always living to make intercession" for those who draw near to God through Him (Hebrews 7:25).

18.resume: Job, a man of integrity, loses everything: his possessions, his children, his health. His friends accuse him, he cries out to God, and God finally answers him—not with an explanation, but by revealing himself.
18.auteur: Unknown. Jewish tradition has proposed Moses; the book itself says nothing about its author.
18.date: The story takes place in ancient times, comparable to the patriarchs' era: Job himself offers sacrifices for his family, his wealth is counted in herds, and he lives another 140 years after his trial (Job 42:16). The date of writing remains unknown.
18.destinataires: Everyone who wonders why the righteous suffer—and who needs to learn that you can cry out to God without letting him go.
18.contexte:
Job lives in the land of Uz; he is "blameless and upright," he fears God and turns away from evil (Job 1:1). In a heavenly scene, Satan claims that Job loves God only for his blessings. God permits the trial. Job loses everything, but he knows nothing of what has taken place in heaven.

Three friends come to comfort him, then accuse him: if he is suffering, it's because he has sinned. Job protests his innocence and demands an audience with God. A fourth, Elihu, then speaks. Finally, the Lord answers Job from the midst of the storm (Job 38:1): he does not give an explanation, he reveals himself in his greatness. Job is silent, humbles himself, and God restores him—while his friends are rebuked for not speaking of him rightly (Job 42:7).
plan: The Dialogue with His Three Friends
God Answers from the Midst of the Storm
themes: Suffering is not always the punishment for wrongdoing: Job is righteous, yet he suffers (Job 1:1).
God owes no account to mankind, but he makes himself known to him (Job 42:5).
Job's friends had a tidy theology, and they were wrong (Job 42:7).
In the darkest night of his suffering, Job declares that his Redeemer lives (Job 19:25).

versets.t: and said, 'Naked I came from my mother's womb, and naked shall I return there. The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord!'
For I know that my Redeemer lives, and He shall stand at last on the earth.
I have heard of You by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees You.

18.christ: Job demands an arbiter who can lay his hand on both God and himself (Job 9:33), and he declares: "I know that my Redeemer lives" (Job 19:25). Jesus is that mediator between God and humanity: the only truly righteous one, who suffered without deserving it, and who lives forever.

19.accroche: The Prayer Book of God's People
19.resume: One hundred fifty prayers and songs, written to be sung in the temple and prayed daily. Every emotion of the soul is here: praise, trust, distress, anger, repentance, thanksgiving.
19.auteur: Multiple authors. The titles attribute 73 psalms to David; others are by Asaph, the sons of Korah, Solomon, Heman, Ethan, and Psalm 90 by Moses. Many are anonymous.
19.date: Composed over nearly a millennium, from Moses (Psalms 90:1) until after the exile to Babylon (Psalms 137:1), then gathered into a single collection.
19.destinataires: God's people gathered for worship, and each believer in personal prayer.
19.contexte:
The Psalms are the prayers of Israel, and Jesus prayed them. You'll find hymns of praise, cries for help, confessions of sin, songs of pilgrimage, royal psalms. Nothing is hidden from God: you can tell Him your joy as well as your anger or your sense of abandonment.

The collection is divided into five books, each ending with a blessing, perhaps reflecting the five books of Moses. It opens with the blessed man who meditates on the Lord's law day and night (Psalms 1:2) and closes in an explosion of praise: "Let everything that has breath praise the Lord!" (Psalms 150:6).
plan: Book I: mainly psalms of David
Book II: the sons of Korah and David
Book III: Asaph and the crisis of the people
themes: God is praised for who He is and for what He has done (Psalm 103:2).
You can cry out to God in your distress, and many of these cries end in trust (Psalm 13:6).
God's Word illuminates your path step by step (Psalm 119:105).
Several psalms announce the king chosen by God, the Messiah (Psalm 2:7).

versets.t: Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for You are with me; Your rod and Your staff, they comfort me.
God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.
Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path.
Let everything that has breath praise the Lord! Praise the Lord!

19.christ: Jesus said the Psalms spoke of Him (Luke 24:44). On the cross, He prayed Psalm 22: "My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?" (Matthew 27:46). Psalm 110 announces the King seated at the right hand of God, and Peter sees in Psalm 16 the announcement of the resurrection (Acts 2:27).

20.resume: A collection of advice and sayings to help you live wisely: how to speak, work, manage money, choose friends, and live with family. The foundation of everything: the fear of the Lord.
20.auteur: Primarily Solomon (Proverbs 1:1), who spoke three thousand proverbs (1 Kings 4:32). The book also contains "the words of the wise" (Proverbs 22:17), proverbs of Solomon collected later by the men of King Hezekiah (Proverbs 25:1), and the words of Agur and King Lemuel.
20.date: The core material dates back to the 10th century B.C., under Solomon; the collection was expanded in the time of Hezekiah, around 700 B.C.
20.destinataires: Young people first—the book often addresses "my son"—and anyone who wants to learn to live according to God.
20.contexte:
The book opens with long speeches from a father to his son (chapters 1-9). Wisdom is personified here as a woman calling out in the streets, in stark contrast to the immoral woman who seduces and leads to death.

Then come hundreds of short proverbs, often built in parallel or contrast: the wise and the foolish, the lazy and the diligent, the righteous and the wicked. The foundation is set from the start: "The fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge" (Proverbs 1:7). The book ends with the portrait of a virtuous woman (Proverbs 31:10).
plan: A Father's Advice to His Son
Agur, Lemuel, and the Virtuous Woman
themes: True wisdom begins with respect for God (Proverbs 1:7).
Trust in the Lord rather than in your own understanding (Proverbs 3:5).
The tongue has the power to wound or to heal (Proverbs 12:18).
Everything flows from the heart—guard it well (Proverbs 4:23).

versets.t: The fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge; fools despise wisdom and instruction.
Trust in the Lord with all your heart, and do not lean on your own understanding; acknowledge him in all your ways, and he will make straight your paths.
Guard your heart above all else, for it is the wellspring of life.
Train up a child in the way he should go; even when he is old, he will not depart from it.

20.christ: The Wisdom that calls to people and was present with God at creation (Proverbs 8:30) takes on a face in Jesus, in whom "are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge" (Colossians 2:3). Paul tells us: Christ has been made for us wisdom (1 Corinthians 1:30).

21.resume: A wise man investigates the meaning of life "under the sun." Knowledge, pleasure, work, wealth: everything passes like a vapor. His conclusion: receive each day as a gift from God and fear Him.
21.auteur: "The Preacher, son of David, king in Jerusalem" (Ecclesiastes 1:1), whom tradition identifies as Solomon. Yet Solomon's name never appears, and some see in it a later sage speaking in the guise of the great king.
21.date: In the 10th century BC if the book is by Solomon; otherwise later—the question remains debated.
21.destinataires: Everyone seeking meaning in life and no longer satisfied with easy answers.
21.contexte:
"Ecclesiastes" translates the Hebrew word Qohéleth: "one who speaks to the assembly." He has tried everything—knowledge, pleasure, great works, wealth—and his conclusion returns like a refrain: "Vanity of vanities, all is vanity" (Ecclesiastes 1:2). The Hebrew word evokes a vapor, a mist that dissipates.

This is not a despairing book; it is a lucid one. It invites you to eat your bread with joy, to enjoy the life God gives, to remember your Creator in your youth. And it concludes: "Fear God and keep His commandments, for this is man's all" (Ecclesiastes 12:13). Note: The Segond numbers the end of the book differently; this well-known verse is elsewhere called 12:15.
themes: Nothing under the sun can satisfy the human heart (Ecclesiastes 1:2).
God has set a time for every matter (Ecclesiastes 3:1).
To eat, drink, and find joy in your work is a gift from God (Ecclesiastes 3:13).
The final word of the book: fear God and obey Him (Ecclesiastes 12:13).

versets.t: To everything there is a season, a time for every purpose under heaven…
He has made everything beautiful in its time. Also He has put eternity in their hearts, except that no one can find out the work that God does from beginning to end.
Remember now your Creator in the days of your youth, before the difficult days come, and the years draw near when you say, "I have no pleasure in them"…
Let us hear the conclusion of the whole matter: Fear God and keep His commandments, for this is man's all.

21.christ: Ecclesiastes shows that nothing "under the sun" satisfies, while God has placed in the human heart "eternity" (Ecclesiastes 3:11). Jesus comes from beyond the sun to bring what does not pass away: "I have come that they may have life, and that they may have it to the full" (John 10:10).

22.resume: A love poem between a beloved and a young woman: desire, longing, separation, and reunion. The book celebrates human love as a gift from God.
22.auteur: The title attributes it to Solomon (Song of Songs 1:1). The Hebrew expression can also mean "dedicated to Solomon."
22.date: 10th century BC if the poem is by Solomon.
22.destinataires: Israel; in Jewish tradition, the Song of Songs is read each year during Passover.
22.contexte:
The title means "the song of songs." Two main voices speak to each other: the beloved and his beloved, the Shulamite, with a chorus in the background, the daughters of Jerusalem. The language is poetic and sensual, filled with images of gardens, vineyards, perfumes, and animals.

The book celebrates human love and desire within commitment as a good creation of God: "Love is as strong as death" (Song of Songs 8:6). Throughout the centuries, both Jews and Christians have also read in it an image of the love between God and his people, between Christ and the Church.
plan: The Wedding Procession and Wedding Feast
The Beauty of the Beloved and the Power of Love
themes: Human love is part of what God created "very good."
My beloved is mine, and I am his (Song of Songs 2:16).
Do not awaken love before it is ready: desire knows how to wait (Song of Songs 2:7).
Many waters cannot quench love (Song of Songs 8:7).

versets.t: My beloved is mine, and I am his; He feeds his flock among the lilies.
Set me as a seal upon your heart, As a seal upon your arm; For love is as strong as death, Jealousy is cruel as the grave; Its flames are flames of fire, A most vehement flame of the Lord.
Many waters cannot quench love, Nor can the rivers overflow it; If a man would give for love All the wealth of his house, It would be utterly despised.

22.christ: The New Testament describes the Church as the bride of Christ, whom he loved and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25). The Song of Songs sets the tone: a love that seeks, that longs, and that "many waters cannot quench" (Song of Songs 8:7).

23.accroche: The Holy One of Israel Saves
23.resume: Isaiah announces judgment on Judah and the nations, but also consolation: the return from exile, the Servant who suffers for others, and new heavens and a new earth.
23.auteur: Isaiah, son of Amoz (Isaiah 1:1), prophet in Jerusalem. Many scholars attribute chapters 40 to 66 to later disciples; however, the New Testament quotes both sections under the name of Isaiah (John 12:41).
23.date: His ministry begins in the year of King Uzziah's death (Isaiah 6:1), around 740 BC, and continues under Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, extending past 701 BC.
23.destinataires: Judah and Jerusalem; the second part also addresses the exiles to come.
23.contexte:
Isaiah ministers in Jerusalem for more than forty years, during the time when Assyria crushes the northern kingdom and threatens Judah. He receives his calling through a vision of the Lord seated on His throne, surrounded by seraphim crying out: "Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of hosts!" (Isaiah 6:3). He calls the kings to trust in God rather than in political alliances.

The first part (chapters 1 to 39) announces judgment, but also a child-king, Emmanuel. The second opens with "Comfort, comfort My people" (Isaiah 40:1): it speaks of the return from exile, the suffering Servant, and a renewed creation. He is the prophet most quoted in the New Testament.
plan: The judgment of the earth and salvation
themes: God is "the Holy One of Israel," a title that appears throughout the book (Isaiah 1:4).
Those who trust in the Lord renew their strength (Isaiah 40:31).
An innocent servant bears the sin of others (Isaiah 53:5).
God will create new heavens and a new earth (Isaiah 65:17).

versets.t: Also I heard the voice of the Lord, saying: "Whom shall I send, and who will go for Us?" Then I said, "Here am I! Send me."
For unto us a Child is born, unto us a Son is given; and the government will be upon His shoulder. And His name will be called Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace.
But those who wait on the Lord shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings like eagles, they shall run and not be weary, they shall walk and not faint.
But He was wounded for our transgressions, He was bruised for our iniquities; the chastisement for our peace was upon Him, and by His stripes we are healed.
"For My thoughts are not your thoughts, nor are your ways My ways," says the Lord.

23.christ: Isaiah has been called "the fifth gospel." He announces the child called Emmanuel (Isaiah 7:14)—Matthew sees in this the virgin birth of Jesus (Matthew 1:23)—the child named "Mighty God" and "Prince of Peace" (Isaiah 9:6), and the Servant "wounded for our transgressions" (Isaiah 53:5). In Nazareth, Jesus reads Isaiah 61 and declares: "Today this Scripture passage that you just heard is fulfilled" (Luke 4:21).

24.resume: For forty years, Jeremiah announces the fall of Jerusalem to a people who refuse to listen. Persecuted, he weeps and complains to God—and through him, God promises a new covenant.
24.auteur: Jeremiah, son of Hilkiah, a priest of Anathoth (Jeremiah 1:1). His secretary Baruch wrote down his words at his dictation (Jeremiah 36:4).
24.date: From the thirteenth year of King Josiah, in 627 BC (Jeremiah 1:2), until after the destruction of Jerusalem in 586 BC.
24.destinataires: Judah and Jerusalem, then the exiles in Babylon, to whom Jeremiah writes a letter (Jeremiah 29:1), and the neighboring nations.
24.contexte:
Jeremiah is called while still young, under King Josiah. For forty years, he announces a message no one wants to hear: Babylon will come, Jerusalem will fall, you must surrender. He is beaten, placed in stocks, thrown into a muddy cistern, accused of treason. He wants to be silent, but the word of God is in him like a burning fire (Jeremiah 20:9).

Yet at the heart of the book shines a promise: a new covenant, where God will write his law in hearts (Jeremiah 31:33). To the exiles, he writes that God has "plans of peace, not of disaster" for them (Jeremiah 29:11). After Jerusalem's fall, Jeremiah is forcibly taken to Egypt by the survivors.
themes: God knew Jeremiah before he was even born (Jeremiah 1:5).
The heart is deceitful above all things; it needs to be renewed (Jeremiah 17:9).
Jeremiah remains faithful even when everyone turns against him (Jeremiah 20:9).
God promises to write His law on hearts (Jeremiah 31:33).

versets.t: Before I formed you in the womb I knew you; before you were born I set you apart; I appointed you as a prophet to the nations.
For I know the plans I have for you, declares the Lord, plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope.

But this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, declares the Lord: I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts. And I will be their God, and they shall be my people.
Call to me and I will answer you, and will tell you great and hidden things that you have not known.

24.christ: The new covenant announced by Jeremiah is the one Jesus inaugurates at his last meal: "This cup is the new covenant in my blood" (Luke 22:20). Hebrews quotes Jeremiah 31 at length to show this (Hebrews 8:8). And like Jeremiah, Jesus wept over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41).

25.resume: Five poems mourn Jerusalem destroyed by Babylon. In the heart of the ruins breaks forth a confession of faith: the Lord's compassions are renewed every morning.
25.auteur: The book does not name its author. Tradition attributes it to Jeremiah, a witness to the fall of Jerusalem, who had already composed laments (2 Chronicles 35:25).
25.date: Shortly after the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple, around 586 B.C.
25.destinataires: The survivors of Judah, so they could put words to their pain before God.
25.contexte:
The temple burned, the city lay in ruins, children died of hunger, the people were deported. Lamentations gives voice to the unspeakable. The first four poems are acrostics: each stanza begins with a letter of the Hebrew alphabet, as if to express the pain from A to Z, in a complete and ordered way.

The book acknowledges that this disaster is the fruit of the people's sin. But at the very center of the book, amid the ruins, hope breaks forth: "The Lord's compassions never fail; His mercies never end; they are new every morning" (Lamentations 3:22-23).
plan: Hope in the Midst of Despair
themes: The Bible gives words to pain and complaint before God.
The fall of Jerusalem was not an accident: it was foretold.
Even at the depths of the abyss, God's faithfulness remains great (Lamentations 3:23).
Turn us back to You, and we will return (Lamentations 5:21).

versets.t: The Lord's compassions never fail; His mercies are not exhausted. They are new every morning; great is Your faithfulness.
It is good to wait quietly for the salvation of the Lord.
Restore us to Yourself, O Lord, that we may return; renew our days as in days of old.

25.christ: Jesus wept over Jerusalem, announcing its future destruction (Luke 19:41). On the cross, He bore to the end the anger that Lamentations describes, so that God's compassions would be renewed for us every morning.

26.resume: A prophet among the exiles in Babylon, Ezekiel sees God's glory departing from the defiled temple. After Jerusalem's fall, he announces a new heart, bones coming back to life, and a new temple.
26.auteur: Ezekiel, a priest, son of Buzi (Ezekiel 1:3), deported to Babylon with King Jehoiachin. He writes in the first person.
26.date: From the fifth year of Jehoiachin's captivity in 593 B.C. (Ezekiel 1:2) to the twenty-seventh year in 571 B.C. (Ezekiel 29:17).
26.destinataires: The exiles settled near the Kebar River in Babylon, and later all Israel.
26.contexte:
Ezekiel was among the first exiles. One day, by the Kebar River, the heavens open and he beholds the glory of the Lord (Ezekiel 1:1). He announces to the exiles, who still hope for a quick return, that Jerusalem will fall. His messages are often acted out: he lies on his side, shaves his head, does not mourn his wife.

In a vision, he sees God's glory leaving the temple defiled by idolatry (Ezekiel 10:18). After Jerusalem's fall, his message turns around: God will give a new heart, revive the dry bones, and return to dwell in a new temple. The book ends with the city's name: "The Lord Is There" (Ezekiel 48:35).
plan: The Shepherd, the New Heart, and the Bones
themes: God cannot be confined anywhere: His glory appears even in exile (Ezekiel 1:1).
God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked; He desires that they turn from their ways and live (Ezekiel 18:23).
God will remove the heart of stone and give a heart of flesh (Ezekiel 36:26).
The dry bones come to life by the Spirit (Ezekiel 37:5).

versets.t: Do I have any pleasure in the death of the wicked, says the Lord God, rather than that he turn from his ways and live?
I will seek what was lost and bring back what was driven away, bind up the broken and strengthen the sick; but I will destroy the fat and the strong, and feed them in judgment.
I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you; I will take the heart of stone out of your flesh and give you a heart of flesh.
Thus says the Lord God to these bones: Surely I will cause breath to enter into you, and you shall live.

26.christ: Ezekiel announces that God Himself will seek His sheep and give them one shepherd, "My servant David" (Ezekiel 34:23). Jesus takes up the image: "I am the good shepherd" (John 10:11). And the promised Spirit, who makes us live according to God (Ezekiel 36:27), is poured out at Pentecost.

27.resume: Deported to Babylon, Daniel serves in the courts of kings without denying his God. The second half of the book records his visions about the succession of empires and God's eternal reign.
27.auteur: Daniel, according to Jewish and Christian tradition; chapters 7–12 are written in the first person, and Jesus speaks of "the prophet Daniel" (Matthew 24:15). However, many modern scholars date its composition to the second century B.C.
27.date: The narrative spans from the first deportation in 605 B.C. (Daniel 1:1) to the third year of Cyrus, around 536 B.C. (Daniel 10:1).
27.destinataires: Jews in exile and, beyond them, all believers who live out their faith in a society that doesn't share it.
27.contexte:
A young nobleman of Judah, Daniel is taken to Babylon along with his friends Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, renamed Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. Trained at the court of Nebuchadnezzar, they serve the empire without denying their God: they refuse the king's food, the furnace does not burn them, and Daniel continues to pray three times a day at the risk of the lions' den (Daniel 6:10).

The second half of the book records visions about the empires that succeed one another and about God's final reign. Daniel sees coming on the clouds "one like a son of man," to whom is given a kingdom that will never be destroyed (Daniel 7:13-14). A portion of the book, from chapter 2 to chapter 7, is written in Aramaic, the international language of that time.
plan: Daniel and his friends at court
Daniel's prayer and the seventy weeks
themes: Serving without compromise, even when it costs (Daniel 3:17–18).
It is God who brings down and establishes kings (Daniel 2:21).
Daniel's regular prayer is the secret of his steadfastness (Daniel 6:10).
All empires pass away; God's reign endures (Daniel 7:14).

versets.t: He changes the times and the seasons; he removes kings and establishes kings; he gives wisdom to the wise and knowledge to those who have understanding.

If that is the case, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver us out of your hand, O king. But if not, be it known to you, O king, that we do not serve your gods, and we will not worship the gold statue that you have set up.

I saw in the night visions, and behold, with the clouds of heaven there came one like a son of man, and he came to the Ancient of Days and was presented before him. And to him was given dominion and glory and a kingdom, that all peoples, nations, and languages should serve him; his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom one that shall not be destroyed.
And those who are wise shall shine like the brightness of the sky above; and those who turn many to righteousness, like the stars forever and ever.

27.christ: The title Jesus preferred to use of himself, "the Son of Man," comes from Daniel 7. Before the Sanhedrin, he quotes this passage: "you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of power and coming on the clouds of heaven" (Matthew 26:64). This statement is what leads to his condemnation.

28.accroche: The Love That Won't Let Go
28.resume: God calls Hosea to marry a woman who will be unfaithful to him. His family life becomes a living prophecy: Israel betrays her God, but God loves her still and calls her to return.
28.auteur: Hosea, son of Beeri (Hosea 1:1), prophet of the northern kingdom.
28.date: Around 755–715 BC, during the reign of Jeroboam II in Israel and the kings Uzziah through Hezekiah in Judah (Hosea 1:1).
28.destinataires: Israel, the northern kingdom, in its final decades before the fall of Samaria.
28.contexte:
God calls Hosea to marry Gomer, who will be unfaithful to him. Just as Gomer betrays Hosea, Israel betrays the Lord by chasing after Baal. The names of their children carry messages: Lo-Ruhamah, "no compassion," and Lo-Ammi, "not my people" (Hosea 1:9).

Yet Hosea redeems Gomer and takes her back (Hosea 3:2). The book alternates between accusations and heart-wrenching calls of love: "What shall I do with you, Ephraim? … My heart churns within Me" (Hosea 11:8). A few years later, in 722 BC, Samaria falls to Assyria.
themes: God loves His people like a betrayed husband who refuses to give up (Hosea 11:8).
Running after other gods is betraying the One who loves you.
My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge (Hosea 4:6).
Return to the Lord, and He will forgive (Hosea 14:2).

versets.t: My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge. Because you have rejected knowledge, I also will reject you from being priest for Me; because you have forgotten the law of your God, I also will forget your children.
For I desire mercy and not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.
How can I give you up, Ephraim? How can I hand you over, Israel? How can I make you like Admah? How can I set you like Zeboim? My heart churns within Me; My compassions are kindled together.
Take words with you, and return to the Lord. Say to Him, "Take away all iniquity; receive us graciously, for we will offer the sacrifices of our lips.

28.christ: Jesus quotes Hosea twice: "I desire mercy and not sacrifice" (Matthew 9:13). Matthew sees in "I called My Son out of Egypt" (Hosea 11:1) a foreshadowing of Jesus's childhood (Matthew 2:15). And Paul applies to the Church God's promise of calling "My people" those who were not His people (Romans 9:25).

29.accroche: I Will Pour Out My Spirit
29.resume: After a devastating locust invasion, Joel calls the people to return to God with all their hearts and announces the day when God will pour out His Spirit on all flesh.
29.auteur: Joel, son of Pethuel (Joel 1:1). Nothing else is known about him.
29.date: Uncertain: the book mentions no king. Proposals range from the 9th to the 5th century BC.
29.contexte:
An unprecedented locust invasion has ravaged the land: no more harvests, no more offerings at the temple. Joel reads in this a warning and an announcement of the "day of the Lord." He calls all the people, from elders to infants, to fasting and repentance: "Tear your hearts and not your garments" (Joel 2:13).

Then comes the promise: God will restore the years the locust has devoured (Joel 2:25), and above all He will pour out His Spirit on all flesh—sons and daughters, elders and young people, servants and maidservants (Joel 2:28-29).
plan: The Day of the Lord and Return to God
The Judgment of Nations and Blessing
themes: God does not want outward gestures but torn hearts (Joel 2:13).
A day of judgment and salvation, when God intervenes in history.
God can restore the lost years (Joel 2:25).
The Spirit is no longer reserved for a few prophets (Joel 2:28).

versets.t: Tear your hearts and not your garments, and return to the Lord your God; for He is gracious and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, and He relents over disaster.
I will restore to you the years that the swarming locust has eaten, the hopper, the destroyer, and the cutter, my great army, which I sent among you.
And it shall come to pass afterward that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, and your young men shall see visions.

And it shall come to pass that everyone who calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved. For in Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there shall be those who escape, as the Lord has said, and among the survivors shall be those whom the Lord calls.

29.christ: On the day of Pentecost, Peter explains what is happening by quoting Joel: "this is what was spoken by the prophet Joel" (Acts 2:16). The promised Spirit is poured out by the risen Jesus, and "everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved" (Romans 10:13).

30.accroche: Let Justice Roll Down Like a River
30.resume: A shepherd from Judah is sent to the northern kingdom, then wealthy and religious. He denounces a prosperity built on the crushing of the poor and a worship without justice.
30.auteur: Amos, one of the shepherds of Tekoa (Amos 1:1), who was "neither a prophet, nor a son of a prophet" (Amos 7:14).
30.date: Around 760 BC, under Uzziah in Judah and Jeroboam II in Israel, "two years before the earthquake" (Amos 1:1).
30.destinataires: Israel, the northern kingdom, and in particular its wealthy and religious leaders.
30.contexte:
Amos comes from the south, but God sends him to preach in the north, especially at Bethel, the great sanctuary of the kingdom. Under Jeroboam II, Israel experiences unprecedented prosperity: ivory houses, lavish religious feasts. But they sell the poor "for a pair of sandals" (Amos 2:6) and justice is bought and sold.

Amos denounces a religion without justice: God despises the feasts of those who crush the weak. "Let justice roll down like waters, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream" (Amos 5:24). The priest of Bethel drives him away. Yet the book ends with a promise: God will restore the house of David (Amos 9:11).
plan: Judgments Against the Nations and Against Israel
Five Visions and the Final Promise
themes: God sees how you treat the poor (Amos 2:6).
The worst judgment: no longer hearing the word of the Lord (Amos 8:11).
After judgment, God will restore the house of David (Amos 9:11).

versets.t: Therefore thus will I do unto thee, O Israel: and because I will do this unto thee, prepare to meet thy God, O Israel.
But let justice roll down like waters, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream.
Behold, the days come, saith the Lord God, that I will send a famine in the land, not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the Lord.

30.christ: At the Council of Jerusalem, James quotes Amos: God will restore the tent of David, "so that the rest of men may seek the Lord, and all the Gentiles who are called by my name" (Acts 15:17). In Jesus, Son of David, the promise is fulfilled and the door opens to the Gentiles.

31.resume: The shortest book of the Old Testament announces the fall of Edom, which had rejoiced in Jerusalem's misfortune, and the ultimate victory of God's kingdom.
31.auteur: Obadiah, whose name means "servant of the Lord." Nothing else is known about him.
31.date: Probably shortly after Babylon's conquest of Jerusalem in 586 BC, when Edom took advantage of Judah's disaster.
31.destinataires: Edom, and Judah, who needed to know that God saw the injustice they had suffered.
31.contexte:
The book contains only twenty-one verses. It targets Edom, the people descended from Esau, Jacob's brother. When Jerusalem was plundered, Edom watched, rejoiced, and even handed over the fugitives (Obadiah 1:14)—a betrayal between brothers.

Obadiah announces that Edom's pride, perched in its rocky heights like an eagle in its nest, will be brought low (Obadiah 1:3-4). "It will be done to you as you have done" (Obadiah 1:15). And the book closes with a certainty: "the kingdom will be the Lord's" (Obadiah 1:21).
plan: The Day of the Lord and God's Kingdom
themes: Pride makes you believe you're beyond reach (Obadiah 1:3).
Rejoicing in your brother's misfortune is serious in God's eyes (Obadiah 1:12).
The last word belongs to the Lord (Obadiah 1:21).

versets.t: For the Day of the Lord upon all the nations is near; As you have done, it shall be done to you; Your deeds shall return upon your own head.
Then saviors shall come to Mount Zion to judge the mountains of Esau, and the kingdom shall be the Lord's.

31.christ: Obadiah announces deliverers on Mount Zion and a kingdom that will belong to the Lord (Obadiah 1:21). Jesus begins His ministry proclaiming this kingdom: "The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand" (Mark 1:15).

32.resume: Jonah flees God's command to preach to Nineveh, the enemy capital. Swallowed by a great fish, he finally obeys—and when Nineveh repents, it's Jonah who becomes angry.
32.auteur: The book does not name its author; it speaks of Jonah in the third person. Jonah, son of Amitthai, is a prophet known from the time of Jeroboam II (2 Kings 14:25).
32.date: The story takes place around 780-760 BC, when Assyria is the threatening superpower.
32.destinataires: Israel, who needed to learn that God's mercy extends even to their enemies.
32.contexte:
God sends Jonah to Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, Israel's cruelest enemy. Jonah flees in the opposite direction, toward Tarshish. A storm, pagan sailors who pray, a great fish: Jonah, swallowed up, prays from the depths of the abyss (Jonah 2:3) and is returned to dry land.

In Nineveh, his preaching boils down to a single sentence, and the entire city repents, from the king to the animals. God forgives (Jonah 3:10). Jonah, however, is furious: he knew that God is "compassionate and merciful" (Jonah 4:2). The book ends with an open question from God: should I not have compassion on this great city? (Jonah 4:11)
themes: God loves even those we consider our enemies (Jonah 4:11).
You cannot escape God, but you can return to him (Jonah 2:3).
God sees a change in conduct and forgives (Jonah 3:10).
You can obey God without sharing his heart: the book questions Jonah, and us with him.

versets.t: Then Jonah prayed to the Lord his God from the fish's belly. And he said: "I cried out to the Lord because of my affliction, And He answered me. Out of the belly of Sheol I cried, And You heard my voice."
Then God saw their works, that they turned from their evil way; and God relented from the disaster that He had said He would bring upon them, and He did not do it.

And should I not pity Nineveh, that great city, in which are more than one hundred and twenty thousand persons who cannot discern between their right hand and their left hand, and also much livestock?

32.christ: Jesus speaks of the "sign of Jonah": as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the fish, so the Son of Man will be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth (Matthew 12:40). And He adds: "something greater than Jonah is here" (Matthew 12:41).

33.resume: A prophet from the Judean countryside, Micah denounces the injustice of the powerful in Samaria and Jerusalem, and announces a ruler who will come from the small town of Bethlehem.
33.auteur: Micah of Moresheth (Micah 1:1), a village in Judah; he was a contemporary of Isaiah.
33.date: Under the kings Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah (Micah 1:1), around 735–700 BC.
33.destinataires: Samaria and Jerusalem, the capitals of the two kingdoms.
33.contexte:
Micah comes from the countryside. Like Amos, he denounces the powerful who seize the fields of others, the judges who accept bribes, the prophets who preach for money. He announces the fall of Samaria, and even that of Jerusalem. A century later, elders will recall that this prophecy led King Hezekiah to repentance (Jeremiah 26:18–19).

But Micah also announces a ruler who will come from Bethlehem, "little among the thousands of Judah" (Micah 5:1). And he sums up all of God's will in one famous sentence: practice justice, love mercy, and walk humbly with your God (Micah 6:8).
plan: The Coming Kingdom and the Ruler from Bethlehem
themes: God demands justice, mercy, and humility (Micah 6:8).
Woe to those in leadership who exploit the people they should protect.
The Deliverer will come from a small village (Micah 5:2).
Who is a God like You, who pardons iniquity? (Micah 7:18)

versets.t: But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, though you are little among the thousands of Judah, yet out of you shall come forth to Me the One to be Ruler in Israel, whose goings forth are from of old, from everlasting.
He has shown you, O man, what is good; and what does the Lord require of you but to do justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?
Who is a God like You, pardoning iniquity and passing over the transgression of the remnant of His heritage? He does not retain His anger forever, because He delights in mercy.
